RECONSTRUCTED TEXT — Open Library search-inside, 2026-09-06
===========================================================
TWO FAMILY MEMOIRS THAT DESCRIBE KANAWANA FROM OUTSIDE IT — one from the late 1920s, one from the
late 1990s. Neither is a camp document; both are books about something else, written by a relative
of a camper, in which the camp appears because it was part of the life being described.

NOT SCANS. Both books are lending-restricted on the Internet Archive; neither has been read. Each
passage below was assembled by walking overlapping twelve-word windows returned by
https://openlibrary.org/search/inside.json (contract at f_4933), to a sentence or subject boundary
in both directions. Page images on lending-restricted items return HTTP 403 with an HTML body even
with the item's own details page sent as Referer — a different failure from the missing-Referer trap
that returns a 43-byte transparent GIF under HTTP 200. The OCR's own line-break hyphens ("improv¬
ing", "sum- mer") are left in place as evidence of where the scan broke.

BOTH ITEMS WERE FOUND BY QUERYING "Kamp Kanawana" RATHER THAN "Kanawana". p_430's item list was
compiled from the bare-"Kanawana" enumeration and did not have either of the two books added to the
project on 2026-09-06 from the same query; the camp has spelled its own name two ways for a century
and both spellings have to be run.


===============================================================================
ITEM 1. Jan Elvin, THE BOX FROM BRAUNAU: IN SEARCH OF MY FATHER'S WAR
        (New York: AMACOM/American Management Association, 2009). ISBN 9780814410493.
        Internet Archive: boxfrombraunauin0000elvi — scan leaf 296; the index entry reads
        "Kamp Kanawana, 24", so this is the boyhood chapter, "The golden boy".
        Subject of the book: the author's father, WILLIAM JOHN ELVIN, US 80th Infantry Division.
===============================================================================

RECOVERED PASSAGE (continuous; two runs, joined where they overlap):

    "In 1926, when Dad was eight and the family had spent two years in Maryland, Jim announced that
    the company was dispatching him to Quebec to help purchase and install the machinery for a new
    plant in Drummondville on the Saint-Fran[ç]ois River. The fam[ily] ... found the cold, biting
    winter in Drummondville exhilarating. Taxi drivers removed their ...

    ... [when he] wasn't in the mood for company, he'd send the whip back at them. Every summer, Dad
    and Georgie went off to Kamp Kanawana, a YMCA camp located on a remote lake in the Laurentians
    north of Montreal — one of what seemed to my father to be an endless series of thousands. The
    first time Georgie went, he was supposed to spend a week there but got so homesick he wouldn't
    stay. Dad stayed two weeks, improv[ing] his swimming to the point where he finally made it
    across the lake. On the last day of camp, early in the morning, all the campers observed the
    camp ritual of jumping into the cool lake bare naked. Each Sunday in Drummondville, they'd
    dress up for church. ..."

WHAT IT GIVES, IN ORDER OF WORTH:

1. A CAMP RITUAL THIS PROJECT DOES NOT HAVE. "On the last day of camp, early in the morning, all the
   campers observed the camp ritual of jumping into the cool lake bare naked." The KB holds a
   morning dip from the camp's own early literature — reveille at 6.30, physical exercises, then the
   dip — but not a LAST-DAY, WHOLE-CAMP, undressed one, and not the word "ritual" for it. The camp's
   own publications would have had every reason not to print this and every reason to print the
   6.30 dip, which is exactly why an outside memoir is worth reading.

2. A DATE BRACKET. The family arrives in Quebec in 1926, the father being eight; "every summer, Dad
   and Georgie went off to Kamp Kanawana" therefore begins in or after 1927 and runs through the
   family's Drummondville years. That is the Harold Cross era — Cross put up the totem pole in 1927.

3. A CATCHMENT FACT. An AMERICAN family, moved to DRUMMONDVILLE for an industrial posting, sending
   two boys to the MONTREAL YMCA's camp a hundred kilometres away, every summer. Drummondville is
   not Montreal and the Elvins were not Montrealers. Whatever channel carried them to Kanawana —
   the company, the local Y, an English-speaking congregation — is not in the passage, and is a
   question this project had not thought to ask.

4. A CAMPER'S OWN MEASURE OF SUCCESS: swimming across the lake, in two weeks, at eight or nine.

WHAT IT DOES NOT GIVE: a year for any particular summer, a section or tent, a counsellor's name, or
the brother's full name ("Georgie"). The father's name comes from the book's own subject heading,
not from this passage.


===============================================================================
ITEM 2. Janet Torge, DEAR SAM: GRIEVING THE DEATH OF MY SON
        (iUniverse, 27 May 2007). ISBN 9780595423835.
        Internet Archive: dearsamgrievingd0000jane — scan leaf 150.
        The subject is SAM LAZARUS (1978–2004), who already has an article in this wiki.
===============================================================================

A NOTE ON HOW THIS WAS READ, BEFORE THE TEXT. This is a mother's book about her son's death, written
in the form of letters to him. It is published, in print, under her name, with his name in the
title; she chose to make it public and this project is not disclosing anything she did not. But
there is a difference between reading a published book and mining a grieving parent's private
sentences for data, and the difference is how far you walk. The walk here was stopped at the camp
material and at the sentence that places it, and was not extended into the surrounding chapters. The
four windows the index surfaced are all recorded; nothing found was withheld. NO EMBARGO APPLIES:
this is not a personal assessment of a private individual held in a confidential record, it is a
published memoir about a person this wiki already documents, and the 2026-09-03 amendment's default
is written for the former.

RECOVERED PASSAGES:

(a) The CIT application and the summer that followed — continuous:

    "... [he wanted] to be a teacher, but he wanted out of school, not back in again. His employment
    options in Montreal were severely limited by his poor grasp of French. To escape the decision
    about what to do next, he applied for a position as a counselor-in-training at Kamp Kanawana,
    the place he had spent practically every summer since he was eight, and was accepted. That
    summer was terrific. Sam was considered a good counselor with the kids, especially the younger
    ones, who called him 'Daddy' and ran to him whenever a bout of homesickness came over them. He
    was able to share with them a child's enthusiasm for the outdoors while using a firm, older hand
    to keep them in line. However, once camp was [over] ..."

(b) A later summer, from the index window, not walked further:

    "... quickly went off to spend another sum- mer as a camp counselor at Kamp Kanawana but told me
    that when he was finished, he was ..."

(c) The last summer he did not take, from the index window, not walked further:

    "... to spend the summer again as a counselor at Kamp Kanawana, but he continued mak- ing
    arrangements to leave ..."

(d) The funeral, January 2004 — walked one window each way:

    "... [people] share their stories of you. Counselors and kids from Kamp Kanawana are everywhere,
    many at their first funeral. I can see the shock on their young ..."

WHAT IT GIVES:

1. HE WAS A CAMPER FROM AGE EIGHT. Born 3 March 1978, so from the summer of 1986. `sam-lazarus.md`
   Open Question 1 asks what years he attended; this answers the start of it, and "practically every
   summer" answers the shape.

2. THE CIT YEAR CAME AFTER SCHOOL, NOT AT SIXTEEN. He applied "to escape the decision about what to
   do next", having left school and found Montreal employment closed to him by his French. NO YEAR
   IS GIVEN in the recovered text. That is later than a CIT cohort's usual age and is worth
   recording as such rather than converted into a year by arithmetic.

3. WHAT HE WAS LIKE ON STAFF, from someone who was not at camp and is reporting what she was told:
   good with the young ones, called "Daddy" by them, the one homesick children ran to.

4. THAT CAMP CAME TO HIS FUNERAL, in her own sentence, and that for many of the campers there it was
   the first funeral of their lives.

5. A DATING LEAD, NOT AN IDENTIFICATION. The camp's 2003 Junior Boys counsellors plaque carries a
   "Sam L" and a "Sam W" — two Sams disambiguated by initial, which is why neither carries a
   surname. Sam Lazarus died in January 2004, and passage (c) has him meaning to return for the
   following summer, so 2003 would have been his last. That is consistent and it is not proof: the
   plaque gives an initial, and one initial is not a name. Recorded as a lead in the KB, hedged in
   the article, and not folded into the plaque index.

ROUTES NOT TRIED for either book: an authenticated Internet Archive borrow; Google Books snippet
view; a library copy. *Dear Sam* is print-on-demand from iUniverse and is orderable new; *The Box
from Braunau* is a trade book and is widely held.
